title: Decidability of $(\min,+)$-weighted automata determinization
formal: Historical question, now resolved positively: is there a deterministic algorithm that, given any finite min-plus weighted automaton A defined below, halts and decides whether some finite deterministic min-plus weighted automaton D over the same alphabet computes exactly the same function on every finite word? No bound on the number of states of D is supplied.
why: Determinizability identifies which quantitative finite-state computations can discard nondeterministic alternatives without changing any word value. Its resolution supplies a decision boundary relevant to verification and the representation of weighted languages.
status_note: Resolved positively by Almagor, Arbel and Sheinvald: arXiv:2503.23826v1 (31 March 2025), Theorem 20.5, published at SODA 2026, pp. 247–257. The original Automata Exchange question and the finite-word integer-weight model, including initial/final-weight variants, were matched to the theorem. Their LICS 2026 follow-up supplies a primitive-recursive complexity bound. This is published-theorem and model-match verification, not an independent proof audit or proof-assistant certificate.

sentences: A min-plus weighted automaton assigns each finite word the minimum accumulated cost of its runs.
The historical question asks whether the existence of an equivalent deterministic weighted automaton can be decided.
Almagor, Arbel and Sheinvald settled this positively in a 2025 preprint published at SODA 2026.
Their LICS 2026 follow-up supplies a primitive-recursive complexity upper bound.
The card is retained as a resolved record, with unrestricted ambiguity and the endpoint-weight conventions included.

definitions: An automaton consists of a finite nonempty state set Q, a finite nonempty alphabet Σ, initial and final weight functions ι,τ:Q→ℤ∪{+∞}, and a transition weight δ:Q×Σ×Q→ℤ∪{+∞}. A weight +∞ marks an unavailable transition or endpoint. For w=a₁⋯a_m and a state sequence q₀,…,q_m, the run cost is ι(q₀)+Σ_{j=1}^m δ(q_{j−1},a_j,q_j)+τ(q_m), with +∞ absorbing under addition. Define A(w) as the minimum of these costs over all state sequences. For the empty word this is min_q(ι(q)+τ(q)); the minimum of no finite costs is +∞. There are no epsilon transitions, so each run consumes exactly one symbol per transition. Deterministic means that at most one state has finite initial weight and that for every state and input symbol at most one outgoing transition has finite weight. The candidate D may have different states, transitions and integer weights; equivalence requires D(w)=A(w), including agreement at +∞, for every w∈Σ*. Inputs explicitly list the finite sets and weight tables, using signed binary integers and a distinguished infinity symbol. The decision algorithm must terminate on every valid input, rejecting malformed encodings. The all-accepting and unweighted-endpoint presentation used in the main proof is linked to this endpoint-weighted presentation by Remark 8.1 and Appendix B of the cited full paper.
answer_criterion: The original target requires decidability of this language of automata, or a proof of undecidability. It has been settled positively by the cited theorem. Decidability does not mean every weighted automaton is determinizable.

context_blocks.text: This historical question is resolved. Almagor, Arbel and Sheinvald prove that an algorithm can decide whether a min-plus weighted automaton has an equivalent deterministic one. The result appeared as a 2025 preprint and at SODA 2026; a July 2026 follow-up gives a primitive-recursive upper bound on the decision complexity.

A weighted automaton reads a word and accumulates costs along each possible run. Min-plus semantics adds costs along a run, then chooses the smallest total among competing runs. This represents an optimal cost rather than only a yes/no acceptance answer.

For example, one branch can count the a symbols and another the b symbols. Taking the minimum computes min(#a,#b) for every word. Which branch gives the final minimum can change after a long suffix, and this function has no equivalent deterministic weighted automaton. The theorem decides when a deterministic equivalent exists; it does not say that one always does.

The ordinary Boolean subset construction only needs to remember which states remain possible. Here different ways of reaching a state may carry different integer costs. A finite set of original states therefore does not by itself give a finite set of quantitative configurations. This is why eliminating nondeterminism is a separate decision problem.

The 2022 source specifically left unrestricted ambiguity open after results for machines with only polynomially many runs. The later theorem covers the general case. Its model-variant discussion includes initial and final weights, so restricting the displayed proof to all-accepting automata does not leave the historical question unanswered.

The exact optimal running-time complexity is a different question. The 2025 decidability proof did not give a complexity bound, while the LICS 2026 result establishes a primitive-recursive one. This record retains its original decidability target and is hidden from the active reader as resolved.
